quote: then you do not have any beliefs about beavers, true or false
content: This principle is contested, and the standard counterexample is exactly parallel. On Kripke's causal-historical account of reference, a speaker whose only belief about Gödel is "the man who proved the incompleteness of arithmetic" still refers to Gödel even if Gödel stole the proof from Schmidt — reference is secured by a causal chain to a baptism, not by a description the speaker could pass. Putnam's water case, which this sequence discussed two essays ago, makes the same point: speakers in 1750 referred to H₂O while believing nothing true about its nature. So one can be wrong about nearly everything and still be talking about the thing. The footnote also points to a Rorty newspaper piece about Davidson rather than to Davidson, and the principle at issue — that some minimum of true belief is needed to fix content — belongs to Davidson's charity-based semantics, a position with well-known critics rather than a settled result.

quote: There are no-free-lunch theorems in computer science—in a maxentropy universe, no plan is better on average than any other.
content: The no-free-lunch theorems (Wolpert and Macready, IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation 1, 1997) say that search algorithms have identical average performance when averaged over all objective functions, or more precisely over sets closed under permutation. That is not a claim about maximum-entropy universes, and it is famously inapplicable to the structured problem classes that actually arise — which is why the theorems have not stopped machine learning from working. Applied here the analogy also proves too much: it would show equally that a mind with no prior information cannot learn physics, and yet the essay's whole account of induction is that we start with priors that are not uniform. The correct statement is that a learner needs an inductive bias, which is a much weaker claim than the one the sentence is used to license.

quote: if everything about morality is up for grabs, not just the content but the structure and the starting point and the determination procedure
content: The argument here is that without something baked in, "right" would be as contentless as "wakalixes" — and the essay has just supplied its own refutation two essays earlier. "Water" was not contentless in 1700 despite nobody knowing its structure, its starting point, or the procedure that would settle its nature, because reference can be fixed by ostension to a real kind and the details discovered later. Non-naturalist realists take precisely this line about moral terms: Enoch, Parfit, and Huemer all hold that we grasp the concept while its subject matter is not constituted by our dispositions, and Parfit's On What Matters is a book-length attempt to say how. One may reject that view; what one cannot do is rule it out on the grounds that its proponents would then be speaking nonsense, when the same test would have convicted every pre-scientific user of a natural kind term.

quote: Could there be a morality, and ourselves utterly outside its frame of reference?
content: This is the crux, and the argument the essay needs to answer is Horgan and Timmons's Moral Twin Earth (Journal of Philosophical Research 16, 1991), designed against exactly this family of naturalist views. Imagine a community whose moral term is regulated by a different natural property than ours; the naturalist analysis implies they are not disagreeing with us but talking about something else, and yet competent speakers robustly judge that such a community would be in genuine moral disagreement with us, capable of being wrong. That intuition is the data any metaethics has to explain, and the analysis offered here — that their word picks out their framework and ours picks out ours — predicts the opposite. The Pebblesorters essay embraces the consequence; this essay treats it as too obvious to argue for.

quote: I don’t argue by definitions, of course.
content: The essay does argue by definitions, and the preceding paragraphs are the demonstration: the conclusion that you must already know something about morality is derived from the claim that otherwise your moral words would have no meaning. That is a semantic argument in the form Book III's "A Human's Guide to Words" spends twenty-eight essays warning against — establishing a substantive conclusion from what a term must mean for the speaker to be saying anything. The disclaimer does not neutralize it; it identifies it. What the argument shows at most is that a speaker who has no dispositions whatever cannot be interpreted, which is the rock again, and not that the content of morality is fixed by the dispositions a particular speaker happens to have.
